title: Fast k-means Seeding Under The Manifold Hypothesis
claim: Key geometric quantities follow predictable log-log scaling laws with cluster count, with slopes tied to each dataset's intrinsic-dimension exponent.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend, log k on x-axis
description: Two line plots sit side by side. Panel (a), labeled 'β scaling', and panel (b), labeled 'η scaling', both plot a log-scale quantity against log k, with k from about 1.6 to 7. Twelve datasets appear as colored lines with distinct markers: SUSY, HAR, Fashion-MNIST, MNIST-CLIP, CIFAR-10, Reddit, StackExchange and others. The legend gives each dataset's estimated quantization exponent ε, from 0.26 down to 0.06. Lines rise roughly linearly. Datasets with larger ε have steeper slopes, so they fan out. Panel (b) adds shaded confidence bands around each line. Panel (a) is cropped on the left, so its y-axis is missing. Panel (b)'s legend is cut off on the right. Captions use large italic math labels below each panel.
caption: Scaling behavior across datasets
abstract: We study beyond worst case analysis for the $k$-means problem where the goal is to model typical instances of $k$-means arising in practice. Existing theoretical approaches provide guarantees under certain assumptions on the optimal solutions to $k$-means, making them difficult to validate in practice. We propose the manifold hypothesis, where data obtained in ambient dimension $D$ concentrates around a low dimensional manifold of intrinsic dimension $d$, as a reasonable assumption to model real world clustering instances. We identify key geometric properties of datasets which have theoretically predictable scaling laws depending on the quantization exponent $\varepsilon = 2/d$ using techniques from optimum quantization theory. We show how to exploit these regularities to design a fast seeding method called $\operatorname{Qkmeans}$ which provides $O(Ï^{-2} \log k)$ approximate solutions to the $k$-means problem in time $O(nD) + \widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{1+Ï}Ï^{-1}k^{1+Î³})$; where the exponent $Î³= \varepsilon + Ï$ for an input parameter $Ï< 1$. This allows us to obtain new runtime - quality tradeoffs. We perform a large scale empirical study across various domains to validate our theoretical predictions and algorithm performance to bridge theory and practice for beyond worst case data clustering.
